utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. It's been a while since I saw you last in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I can't see you hardly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Ms. Edgerton. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning. And, Your Honours, just regarding yesterday and our discussion about the exhibits, I've had an opportunity to review the details of those exhibits, the ones we described -- or I described as mis-characterised yesterday, and it's going to be far more effective and efficient in terms of time to deal with those in our final brief rather than in court today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now yesterday in talking about the air bomb incident of 7 April, 1995, you said at page 31258: "As far as I can tell, the target of my brigade was only the command post of the 4th and later on the 104th Motorised Brigade," which you said first was in the Hrasnica school and then in the post office in Hrasnica. So my question to you is -- from this: Who made the target decision, was that you or was that someone else?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding specifically air bombs, at the meeting --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. My question is: In this specific case regarding this incident on 7 April, 1995, who made the target decision, you or someone else?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the one.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And that was, as I understand your evidence, based on your understanding of a range of error for the modified air bombs of 10 metres at a distance of 1.000 metres based on those temporary firing tables?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used the term "temporary firing tables," not provisional firing tables because in the Serbian language the word "provisional" is associated with improvisation. Those were temporary firing tables and they were temporary because the combat rules for the use of those assets had not been written yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine. But to go back to my question, my question was that you made that decision based on your understanding of a range of error of 10 metres at a distance of 1.000 metres, as you said in your statement and in your evidence yesterday at page 31250 [sic]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I made the decision to use the air bomb on that target because I estimated that at that moment it was the most profitable target. Let's not forget that in the past three days there were intensive combat actions between 104th Brigade and the 2nd Brigade of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now -- thank you. Now, given the destructive power of these bombs that you talked about yesterday, if the range of error had been any greater than 10 metres at a distance of 1.000 metres, you wouldn't have used it in an urban area, would you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said this yesterday, the command was based at the post office and 50 metres away from it was the so-called school - I'm saying "so-called" because it was not actually a school. So the possibility of error and causing civilian casualties was minimal; that's one thing. And the second thing, I repeat, Mr. Fikret Prevljak, the commander of --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I really hate to interrupt you, but to go back to my question, my question was: If the range of error had been greater than 10 metres at a distance of 1.000 metres - which is what you gave evidence yesterday that you understood it to be - you wouldn't have used this weapon in an urban area, would you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you also said yesterday that you used Plamen rockets as the fuelling agent for these bombs and that was at 31251; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this new modified system incorporating the air bombs also incorporated the existing Plamen rocket system?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, fuel rockets without explosive charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And its accuracy then would have been the same as the existing system?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to have 65 ter number 24335A called up, please. And these are firing tables for the 128-millimetre M63 multiple-rocket system called Plamen, as you see from the first page in front of you. And if we could go over to page 2. Just by the way, Colonel, you know how to read a firing table based on your evidence yesterday; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So if we could have a look, then, at the table here on the left-hand side, most left-hand column, this is the column that, you would agree with me, shows distance; correct? It has metres set out.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in the third line down on the left-hand side we see the figure of 1.000 metres and if we go over to the furthest right-hand column we see -- pardon me, the furthest two right-hand columns, we see the figures for range of error, don't we? And we see that at a range of 1.000 metres, the Plamen rocket has a margin of error of give or take 146 metres by 4 and a half metres. You would agree with me?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And your question is?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You would agree with me? The range of error for the Plamen rocket is plus or minus 146 metres by plus or minus 5 metres.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer that the multiple-rocket launcher has 32 rockets and it's designed mainly for a large-area targets. This firing table is used for that weapon and we only had one fuelled rocket. So this firing table cannot apply to a modified air bomb because this was designed for 32 rockets. If you are aiming at the centre of the target, the error is maximum what is indicated here, but the area covered by the multiple-rocket launcher is much larger than the area covered by the modified air bomb. So you cannot use these figures for comparison with the modified air bomb.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Even taking that into account -- now let me ask you another question. So are you saying that the range of error -- so it's your contention that taking the warhead from the Plamen rocket and attaching a heavier object makes it actually more accurate than the standard produced tested warhead that we've got firing tables for; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to apologise and say that you are putting questions to me that do not fall within my area of knowledge and training. I can only tell you what I know from experience, but I really cannot answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, can we -- Colonel, can you assist. The multiple-rocket launcher fires 32 individual weapons. Each weapon has a propellant and a warhead. Now if I recall from previous evidence, the modified air bombs were propelled by taking four of those rockets, removing the warheads from them, and simply using them as a propellant. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We would need your verbal answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yeah. You're nodding instead of saying "yes." Was the answer to all my questions so far been yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So the ballistics of the single rocket, albeit fired in multiples of 32, and a modified air bomb with four rocket motors, to a layman it sounds it must be different. Was that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: See, the danger is, I think, Ms. Edgerton that you're to some extent comparing apples and oranges it seems to me. To use the firing tables for one weapon system and apply it to a modified and unique system, there may be degrees of inaccuracy, but speaking for myself I don't see how you can use the ballistic tables for one weapon and apply it to another weapon without some form of ballistic expert evidence to back it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I had no intention of taking -- after the Colonel's answers taking this matter any further in any case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- with this witness. I would simply be asking to be able to understand his answers that this document be marked for identification as a Prosecution exhibit, given that it's untranslated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 24335A receives number P6040, MFI'd, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I intervene. The witness said it is much too expert a question for me. That's what he said in line 16. He said this is much too specialised an issue not falling within my area of knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine if the witness confirms that's accurate, and I'd like to move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you also said the house that was hit in Hrasnica on 7 April 1995 was about 20 to 30 metres away from the facility that was your target, and I'd like to call up 65 ter number 24334, please. Now, Colonel, this is an enlargement of a scaled map of Hrasnica marking where you see the green number 10, the location of the incident on 7 April, 1995, and where you see the line with the marking 150 metres, the distance between that location and the Aleksa Santic school, and where you see the line that says 148 metres, the distance between the location of the incident and the former post office. So that's actually not what you said yesterday, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please get the provenance of this map. Who established that it was here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's hear the answer and then you can deal with this matter in your re-examination. She's introduced the scale and the location. It's up to -- it's for the witness to confirm or deny.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the information I got from UNPROFOR and the people who had fled Sarajevo, the air bomb that was launched landed exactly between the school and the post office building - and I'm using these terms "post office" and "school" conditionally. So I cannot comment this information that it landed somewhere on the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I never said it landed somewhere on the road. I told you yesterday it landed on a civilian house. And my question to you is: These two distances being 150 metres between the scene of the incident and the school and 148 metres between the scene of the incident and the post office are not the distances you gave yesterday, are they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what is written here, it would seem so. But I'm telling you, I have information that it did not land there. And I said "the road," because the yellow lines indicate roads. It looks like it landed exactly on the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have this as a Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But how can you argue that number 10 is the point of landing of the air bomb with this witness? Did the witness confirm that number 10 is the point of landing?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Accepted, Your Honour. I'll just move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've just mentioned the information that you had from UNPROFOR and other sources and you mentioned yesterday in your testimony that you heard from UNPROFOR that a Bosnian -- that only one soldier was hit in the incident. And I'd like us to have a look at P2059 in that regard, please. And there should be a translation available for the Colonel. Now, this is a special report from SI-1 entitled: "Large Explosion on Hrasnica on 7th April 1995." And it's a United Nations document, page 1, paragraph 1 says: "As a result of the impact, one civilian female was killed, three civilian females, and one civilian boy were injured ..." So, in fact, this report from UNPROFOR is contrary to the information you said you received yesterday, isn't it, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information I have, in the building that was destroyed and which you claim to be a civilian target -- a civilian building, I said it was a building that housed the guards detail of the 104 Brigade, and even a picture was shown where we could see the legs of a uniformed soldier. So I spoke yesterday about what I'd seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You actually didn't answer my question and my question was: This report from UNPROFOR is contrary to your evidence yesterday to the effect that UNPROFOR told you only one soldier was hit, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is written here is different.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your statement you mentioned at paragraph 26 of your statement - and I see you've got your statement in front of you so you might want to have a look at that paragraph - at paragraph 26 you spoke about civilian casualties in Serb-held territory when you were talking about the psychological state of civilians in your zone of responsibility. And you said the civilian casualties created a big psychological pressure on the civilian population. So you're talking about shelling and sniping civilians in Serb-held territory; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you mean to say that these civilians were scared and insecure?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Frightened of what could happen to them and their family in, for example, going outside because they wouldn't know where the next shell might be coming from?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That war did not last three days - it lasted a long time - and civilians needed to abandon buildings where they lived. Life went on normally almost, market-places were open, shops worked; and what can be established on the basis of my daily reports that I regularly sent to the corps command, in moments when we expected it least Ilidza was hit by mortar shells and artillery shells from Mount Igman causing great casualties. I think you can certainly see that from my reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the number of civilian casualties in Ilidza was about 1.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So that -- that pressure and fear that you're talking about -- well, actually you're talking about terror, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Terror on whose part?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I thought you were talking about civilians in Serb-held territory being terrorised by shelling and sniping?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So -- well, let me ask you this. So being the subject of constant shelling and pervasive sniping would cause this fear anywhere, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Including for civilians in Bosnian-held Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency. Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel, sir.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked whether sniping in urban areas where civilians lived constituted terror. Did you open fire on the Muslim civilian areas in order to terrorise civilians? Why did you open fire in those areas?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ilidza Brigade opened fire but never on civilian targets which were exclusively civilian targets. But I have to say that the school in Dobrinja was not a civilian target because it housed the brigade command. A residential building which is fortified is also not a civilian target. Muslims used those means. They intentionally found shelter in such facilities in order to represent a possible response by our forces as terror.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In that sense, can you tell us who was it who opened the fire first? Who was it who benefitted most from fire being opened in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, as you may well know, on several occasions I don't know how many times a dozen of times cease-fires were agreed. Along the line of subordination, we received orders to strictly adhere to those orders on cease-fire and we did adhere to them. Unfortunately, the Muslim forces did not honour that. They benefitted from the opportunity to provoke us into engaging at the moments when it suited them the most, and it suited them the most when a delegation was about to visit Sarajevo and we really feared that. Whenever somebody arrived, we emphasized for all of our combatants make sure not to engage in any provocations because the Muslims will want you to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also asked about firing air bombs on Hrasnica and a reference was made to a statement was Overgard. Was Overgard a member of UNPROFOR or was he an MO, a military observer? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I'd like to call up 65 ter 15890. Perhaps we should better look at the statement. This is -- the transcript. Let's look at 65 ter 10001.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You received information from a member of the United Nations forces, right, you mentioned that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 10001. Can we take a look at the following page. In English and in Serbian it should be the last paragraph that I'm interested in. I would like to read this in English so that we may control things in Serbian as well. The third and the fourth line from the bottom. [In English] First we went to the police station to pick up Hakija Hasanefendic, the local police inspector. When we came back on site we walked around the site. When we came back we found out that one woman was dead and supposedly some others. I saw some legs under bricks with camouflage trousers and boots." [Interpretation] Is this what you also received by way of information?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the information that I received. He told me that he saw the legs of a soldier in uniform with his own eyes. It says here "I saw some legs."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. He also mentioned that in his evidence, I'm talking about Mr. Overgard, obviously. Do you remember you were shown here an order dated 6 April 1995. That order was issued by General Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that order was in connection with that rocket being fired?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now take a look at 65 ter 16449.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the following page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the document is only two pages long and -- no, this is not the document. I apologise. There may be a mistake. Can we look at D02412 dated the 4th of April, i.e., the same day. D02412 -- I apologise. It is 17 if this is the one, 1217. I apologise for the confusion that I created with the numbers. That's not the number. Instead can we look at P782. P782. It's not P, it's D, D [In English] Defence exhibit [Interpretation] 782. That's it but we are waiting for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, could you please take a look at the date of this document and what was issued on that date by the command of the Sarajevo Corps? The date and the title.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we are looking at 4 April 1995 and it is an order for artillery number 1/95.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You don't have to read it through but could you please take a look at the contents of this document. Why are Muslim forces on Treskavica mentioned? You will find it in the second paragraph of bullet point 2.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the elements of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and other corps such as Herzegovina and Drina Corps should organise defence in the respective zones of their responsibility in order to stop the enemy and keep them in their positions and then to launch counter-attacks on the axis that are mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go to the following page, please. To speed things along I will read. It says here: "Tasks" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not see that on the screen and the accused is reading too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters were not able to keep up with your speed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's simplify things. Colonel, sir, these aerial bombs, are they part of artillery?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The name itself, aerial bombs, implies that aerial bombs are not artillery. However, if modified one may say that they will fall under the category of artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at the fourth bullet point. What about the first paragraph, what kind of defence is this? What does it consist of? And what kind of an enemy infantry advance is this referred to? Where is that? Where are the ends of defence with respect to Hrasnica and Vojkovici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, often your legal adviser objected to various compound questions. Ask one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's simplify things then. What kind of attacks are these and on what axis? What does this document talk about?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, this document talks about attacks along the Muslim axis on the slopes of Igman and Bjelasnica in the direction of the Serbian territory, so we're talking about the areas which were under our control after Lukavac 93 operation and those areas after the agreement was signed were controlled by UNPROFOR. However, it seems that the control was not very good because the Muslim forces benefitted from the withdrawal of our own forces and under the protection of UNPROFOR they wanted to return the territories that they had lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will just read two bullets. "Neutralise the activities of enemy artillery and mortars." And the following one: "After the firing positions are taken, correct -- proceed to make fire adjustment with the battery's main artillery pieces and direct fire artillery pieces upon the first detected target." Did the Muslim forces in Hrasnica in contact with your brigade and the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade have artillery?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about Sokolovic Kolonija along the entire length of the line of contact, was that the same case?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked whether the Army of Republika Srpska closed the airport to humanitarian air-lifts and did they do the same with the roads. What were the main and the most common causes for the closing of roads and airports?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I know, the most common reasons for closing the roads and all the other means of communications were Muslim offensives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember if there was a cease-fire in the area of responsibility of, or rather, in the Sarajevo area in late 1994. That cease-fire was agreed upon in a spectacular manner, as it were?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up D1124.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the attitude of the Army of Republika Srpska and how did the cease-fire reflect on civilians?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand your question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In a nutshell, how did cease-fires reflect on everyday life?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the cease-fires that were signed were used by civilians to make purchases to go to the market-place. They visited each other. To put it simply, during the periods of cease-fire life returned to normal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is Akashi's telegram to Annan which was sent on the 7th of April. The latter was at that time the under-secretary for peacekeeping operations. I am going to read in English. There's no translation. You will receive it through the headphones. [In English] "As with the airport routes ... consent of the parties is the key. Without this the only other option is enforcement. It must be emphasized that during the early part of the cessation of hostilities agreement, life for the average resident in Sarajevo improved considerably. The airport routes were opened, tram services were running, and utilities were beginning to be repaired and maintained. All progress came to a halt due to the refusal of the Bosnian side to attend the central joint commission designed to negotiate, amongst other things, the status of Sarajevo. The flagrant disregard of cessation of hostilities agreement by the BH when they launched two military offensives in Travnik and Stolice areas also contributed considerably to the worsening situation in Sarajevo. "Additionally, the killing of the two Serbian children by sniper fire within Sector Sarajevo influenced and hardened BSA attitudes." [Interpretation] So after life recovered, as it were, how did this activity of the BH army affect the situation regarding humanitarian convoys and transport?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly in such situations when there was a cease-fire agreement that had been signed, supplies became more intensive both in terms of the city and the Serb settlements. More humanitarian aid arrived, but I must say now that often it was abused in the sense of ending up in military warehouses. I have information to the effect that convoys that arrived during cease-fires ended up in logistics bases of the BH army from where this aid was distributed to soldiers, whereas civilians could buy it at the Sarajevo markets, Markale, Grbavica, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Edgerton suggested to you that roads had been closed off even from the month of April. Is it correct, or rather, do you know how the humanitarian aid flowed and is it correct that the roads had been sealed off as of April?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall while I was brigade commander that roads would be closed for more than a few days. In most cases solutions were found because we understood the need to have the civilian population supplied with food.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D1167, could we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since there's no translation I'm going to read it out myself. It's Annan writing to Akashi about what he knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm actually -- Your Honours, this is re-direct examination and I recognise that I haven't given Dr. Karadzic an opportunity to ask this question, but this has been a progressive thing, and my submission is we're actually on the edge of improper re-direct examination because Dr. Karadzic has been spending a great deal of time now reading out evidence rather than effectively seeking the witness's evidence on discrete points that have been raised in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I find it to be a very fair comment, so why don't you put a foundational question first and then if necessary you can visit the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll do my best. This skill still seems to escape me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, it was suggested to you that from April onwards all supplies had been cut off. There's a document here which you cannot read in Serbian, unfortunately, it's dated the 17th of April. And what it says is the complete opposite, that the UNHCR achieved quite a bit. Does this correspond to your own experience?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It seems like Dr. Karadzic may not have understood the point and what we arrived at was effectively a leading question in re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Absolutely. "... what it says is the complete opposite, that the UNHCR achieved quite a bit. Does this to your own experience." This sounds as if you are giving evidence, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will have to find a way to challenge this because documents do actually dispute what the Prosecution had suggested --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As Ms. Edgerton indicated, you can use this passage in your final brief, given that this is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll do my best. Excellency, I would kindly ask you to consider the matter since we've admitted all the transcripts of government meeting, Assembly meetings, Presidency meetings. Also, we should admit all the approvals for convoys every two or three days. There are these documents that allow convoys, approve them, and that is in stark contrast to what has been suggested. If necessary, we can submit this in writing too, if the Trial Chamber believes that would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, what kind of orders did you receive from me and from the top echelons of power as far as convoys are concerned?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that the system of convoys passing through the area of the Ilidza Brigade was quite clear to all of us and as a matter of fact we got a few letters defining that. So convoys were announced and we would let them go in accordance with these announcements.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D283, could I call that up now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this order of mine relates to? You don't have to read it out. Just deal with the essence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again, yes. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- I would submit this is not proper re-direct examination at all, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, would you like to reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I don't see anything wrong at all with this -- doing it the way he's doing it. She's brought up in her cross-examination the issue of obstruction of humanitarian aid. The witness has been asked a foundational question that he's aware of the instructions for foundational aid. And now Dr. Karadzic is going to ask this witness how this document tallies with his understanding of the situation. And if he says that it does and explains how, it can be admitted, which is a perfectly good way to conduct a re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I haven't read the content of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you look at number 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But did he receive this order from Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that's a good question. You can ask him that or if he was aware of it in some way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I wanted -- I told Mr. Karadzic to put some foundational question before putting the document first directly to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: But he did. He asked a foundational question and the witness said he was familiar with the policy concerning that convoys shouldn't been obstructed. Haven't gotten that answer, I don't see anything wrong with him having put the witness -- I don't see that the Prosecution in their direct examinations when the Prosecution witnesses were being called were precluded from asking -- from presenting a document to a witness in these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But take a look at the question Dr. Karadzic posed as a matter of fact. I quote: "Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this order of mine relates to? You don't have to read it out. Just deal with the essence." He doesn't -- he didn't ask whether he knew of the order at the time or whatever. He just wanted to read -- wanted the witness to read and then confirm with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: But look at the question on line 19 right before that. "Colonel, what kind of orders did you receive from me and from the top echelons of power as far as the convoys are concerned?" That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a proper question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's the preliminary question. Having then -- the witness said that we received information, now Dr. Karadzic is asking him: Is this the type of information you received. What's wrong with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In my opinion, I'm speaking for myself, he should have asked whether the witness knew about this order first --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Even if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- instead of asking to confirm the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: But even if the witness doesn't know about this order, if this order is consistent with the instructions that the witness believed he'd received, it should be [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then he can put that question after the first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. I -- honestly I think he did the best -- I think he did it within -- well within acceptable limits, but if you want it done a different way, I don't see any reason why not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, this order of mine, how did it reflect on the orders or instructions that you received from the corps?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orders from the corps command were very specific, that is to say, convoys of humanitarian aid should be allowed to pass according to customary procedure. As I said yesterday, it had been defined clearly and there were never any problems in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The orders of the president, did the corps convey them to units?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Important orders like this one were. I am familiar with this order but not directly in this form. Rather, what I received were the obligations that I had as brigade commander on the basis of this order of yours, and then this became part of the regular procedure that I've already discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me something, I need this for a particular document, how the other side behaved towards us during Christian holidays?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during Christian holidays, we raised the combat-readiness of our units because most often fire was opened at our positions then. That would be their greeting card sent to us. Since the lines were very close that is actually what they would say to us, "We wish you a happy holiday," with gun-fire. We received that but we did not the respond with fire because that was not our custom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did we behave during Islamic holidays?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of instructions that we received from you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3470, I would like to call that up then. May I tender the previous document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it not admitted yet? Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document receives number D2619, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3470 then, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that my orders were sent on to the units. Does it also say here sent to all units and can you read out the first sentence?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. "The Army of Republika Srpska" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no, please. The preamble before that.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Submit to all units. "We hereby forward the integral text of the order of the president of the RS number 01-464/94, dated the 13th of March, 1994."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then my order follows and that's under quotation marks. What does this relate to? Could you please interpret the first, second, and third paragraphs. It hasn't been translated because I didn't know that this would be challenged.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to your order that we exercise maximum restraint in terms of responding to provocations of the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When? On what occasion?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the Muslim holiday, Bajram, the 13th and the 14th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what is the second paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer the question, yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I stood because questions related to the holidays were really not something that was a subject of cross-examination in any regard, Your Honours, and this line of questioning and this document seems to be derived from that. And I think that's not appropriate re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you assist us, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I totally agree with Ms. Edgerton that this issue of the holidays is outside of the scope of the cross-examination. I think the document is admissible for well within the scope of her cross-examination concerning why they were firing, but the aspect of the document that Dr. Karadzic has highlighted I don't think arises from the re-direct -- from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since there is no translation, Excellency, I would like to ask the Colonel about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The first paragraph is all right. It has to do with the Bajram holiday. And what about the other two paragraphs? Could the convoy -- what is the essence of my order that is being conveyed to you by Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You repeated several times that we should let convoys pass through in accordance with the procedure that we received. And it says here that we should not create any problems, but rather that we should observe the procedure involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D3470 receives number D2620, Your Honours, MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last document, although there are many of them --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said in response to a question from Ms. Edgerton that it was not only Republika Srpska or your brigade that stopped convoys, that perhaps convoys were stopped in Herceg-Bosna. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have to recall that Herceg-Bosna bordered the Igman Brigade and was perhaps 10 kilometres away from my positions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get 1D3170.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Karadzic kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you are asked to slow down by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3170. It exists in Serbian and in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the date and who is writing to whom -- all right. We see that. The Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army is addressing the command of the UNPROFOR. Look at the last paragraph. Read it, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in support of the fact that the Muslim side by obstructing the convoys they had used for the past three years is trying to create the impression that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page. In English that's the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Go on, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we zoom in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This supports the fact that the Muslim side preventing convoy movement on the route which has been used for three years wants to make you believe that it is impossible to use the aforementioned route?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it says specifically that the route via Igman is used, which we will never accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Skip the next and then read from "our side."

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Our side will take all necessary measures" -- can you help me because I can't read this copy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll read the first sentence. We don't have to read the rest. "Our side will take all necessary measures in order to provide full safety to the convoys moving through our territory as well as the measures shortening and hastening the procedure for getting clearance. We are surprised that you are blaming the VRS for turning convoys back to Muslim-held territory." Is it consistent with what you said yesterday that the other side was stopping convoys too?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What could be their motivation to stop convoys and why was it not acceptable to us that convoys should go via Igman?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you asked about their possible motivation, did you mean the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I meant the adversary.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wanted to portray us as unco-operative, as wishing to exhaust their population, subject them to attrition, and we did not want the Igman road used because it was the route of supply to their forces. The road Sarajevo-Ilidza-Hadzici was the one used before. They wanted to use the UNPROFOR and get them to use the other road so that they could smuggle in their own equipment. I had information that they even painted over two of their APCs into blue and we did not want to shoot at them because we did not want to take any risks.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document receives number D2621, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel, for your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Colonel Radojcic, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was my pleasure and honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the time, shall we take an early break?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In Your Honour's hands. If we go with the witness summary now, we can just play through until the normal break. My colleague, Ms. West, will be dealing with that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then let's bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, just two brief issues. I'm not sure if you want to do this in the presence of the witness. The first is the warning of which I have not advised the parties of. However, after reflection, I would like that advisement given to the witness. The second is there are five associated exhibits to which I have an objection. I'm not sure if it's more efficient to do this now or later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, why don't we do that. I will hear from you. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honour, I'm focusing on paragraphs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The witness we are talking about is Mr. Bambarez?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a total of 11 associated exhibits and I just have objections to five, and the focus of those five are paragraphs 8, 9, and 10. These are all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was the number of the 65 ter?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: These go from 1D8544 then -45 -46, and then 1D8554 and 1D8555.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And those are five photographs. They are photographs of buildings in Sarajevo, a few of which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. A few of which have some markings on it that were made by the witness. There are a few reasons why I think they should not be included as associated exhibits. The first is they are, for the most part, undated. And I understand that the defence in this case, as regards these particular photos, is that there was a Bosnian Muslim sniper on the building. It would be important to know the date of these photographs because it's not clear to me to which scheduled incidents these photographs are attributed. Secondly, the paragraphs 8, 9, and 10 are inconsistent with each other as regards to the photographs. So, for example, paragraph 8 notes in one of these photographs that a building marked as number 1 did not exist. But then we go to paragraph 9 and it speaks of this 1D8545, which I believe refers to the same building that they refer to in the previous paragraph, and they say part of the building did not exist. But then when I looked at their 92 ter package from a few days ago under 8545, it says a photograph showing the building not present during the war. So the paragraphs in and of themselves are mutually inconsistent. That coupled with a lacking of the dates -- and thirdly, it's just very difficult to understand what exactly the witness means when you read these three paragraphs. I had -- well, it's still unclear to me exactly what it means. So as regards the other exhibits, I have no problem; but as regards these five exhibits, I would ask that they be led live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, the question is whether these are made -- are -- whether they require the exhibits to be admitted to comprehend the statement. It clearly does, otherwise these three paragraphs are meaningless. Any issues as to the unclarity of those are something that can be dealt with in cross-examination, just like any other unclear portions of a witness's statement. So the points that she raises are things that she should take up in her cross-examination but don't go to the issue of whether these are indispensable parts of the actual statement, which they clearly are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But usually would you agree, would you not, that in order to understand what the markings would mean you need to hear live to a certain extent? It's very difficult to follow to understand the meaning of markings made by the witness without his explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And if you - after having read those paragraphs - feel that you would like those to be led live because you don't believe it's clear, then we can definitely do it for that reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I found this to be a perfect timing for a break and then we'll have a break for half an hour and resume at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bambarez. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you start giving evidence, I would like to draw your attention to a particular rule here at the Tribunal. Under this rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the Prosecution or the accused or from the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in such a case the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue -- please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bambarez.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I call up in e-court 1D6904.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see that statement on the screen?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you read that statement and signed it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I offer this package and I will elicit viva voce evidence on the three photographs that the Prosecution has referred to and that the witness has marked. I will do that after reading the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West referred to five photos. Do you mean all of them?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will explain paragraphs 8 and 10 of Mr. Bambarez's statement, or rather, the matters covered by those paragraphs and we will see about the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Can I take this opportunity to express the Chamber's general preference to hear live when the witness is dealing with maps with his or her own markings. In particular, the two photographs dealt with in para 10 with 65 ter numbers 1D8554 and 1D8555, given that they are not familiar with us and the Chamber is not familiar -- aware of the provenance of those two photos, the Chamber was of the opinion that those should be led live with the witness. But it's even better for you to lead with the other remaining three documents -- photos as well. One further thing is that the photo dealt with in para 11, 1D8551, allegedly being the picture of Baba Stijene feature, I have not seen the picture yet but I do not see the point of tendering that photo at all. We have seen a lot of photos of that place and the witness said that there is no -- there were no snipers in that position. Is it not sufficient by the statement itself? So if there's a point in specifically of tendering that photo, you need to lead live with the witness as well. Having said that, I would like you to proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I should now like to read out the summary of Mr. Bambarez's statement in English and then I will lead the evidence. [In English] Zeljko Bambarez is an economic technician by profession from Centar municipality, Sarajevo. When the war began the people in his settlement organised themselves, forming a unit of approximately 25 men establishing a line of disengagement in Zlatiste in front of their settlement which was 99 per cent Serbian. There was no established military unit at that time. After the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was formed, he was appointed commander of the 2nd platoon of the 2nd Command [sic] of the 3rd Battalion in the Romanija Infantry Brigade. In June 1993 his battalion became part of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade. During 1994, Mr. Bambarez spent eight months in Grbavica. His unit comprised local men and the command structure did not include any professional officers. In his statement, Zeljko Bambarez describes the line of separation between the VRS and the BH army as well as the positions held by the two armies. He likewise explained the use of artillery and snipers in his unit as well as their use by the BH army and the passing of humanitarian aid in his area of responsibility as well as the status of electricity and water-supply. In June the 8th -- 9th, 1992, they were tasked with, his own unit, to liberate the Lukavica-Pale communication route. This route had been cut off by Muslim forces which attacked the witness's platoon. They -- Bambarez's unit managed to successfully liberate the route by 17th of June, 1992, and they remained in these positions until 31st of October of the same year. This corridor was being used to transport humanitarian aid to the Muslim side. Zeljko Bambarez's unit secured the route and did not cause any problem or obstructions to such aid. The aforementioned route became at the time unsafe since it was the only road connecting Pale and Sarajevo. Sometimes around October 1992 approximately 50 civilians residing in Serbian territory were killed by Muslim armed forces while travelling along the route. To avoid any further losses of civilian lives, the witness and his platoon tried to move the line of disengagement but failed to do so, losing five men in the process. The witness and his platoon remained at the same position until the end of the war. Zeljko Bambarez also recalls that the mortar positions in his company was in the same spot throughout the war and that it was never within the sectors of Miljevici and Studenkovici or along the road leading to the -- to Studenkovici. In fact, there were never any mortar or artillery positions whatsoever in either of the aforementioned sectors. Furthermore, his platoon never had snipers and his unit was only involved in defence operations, with the sole exceptions of the failed attempt to move the line of disengagement in the Lukavica-Pale corridor. This was the only non-purely defensive operation action in which his unit was involved. They were instructed to save ammunition and refrain from firing for no reason. Zeljko Bambarez explains that never he or any other members of his unit, or their subordinated or superior commands, intended to cause civilian casualties or terrorise civilians in the territory under Muslim control or attack means of public transportation. They never received or issued any verbal or written orders to that effect. Even in those occasions where civilians who remained in the territories under Muslim control were forced to dig trenches for the opposing Muslim forces and whose forced labour posed a direct threat to the unit's position of Mr. Bambarez, his unit followed orders not to fire at civilians. On the contrary, civilians within territory under control of Serbian authorities lived in constant fear due to the attacks by Muslim forces. The first civilian casualty occurred during an enemy shell in 1992. His name was Nedjo Granic, a mentally retarded civilian unfit for combat. Likewise, a young man was killed by a Muslim sniper while in a car near Knjeginac. Furthermore, several Serb civilians in Sarajevo had to flee the area. Zeljko Bambarez also explains that during the war they already had information that civilian features in Sarajevo were being misused and abused by military purposes, such as the Kosevo Hospital, the military hospital, and the city hall, as well as the civilian houses. Likewise, water-supply for the Muslim part of the city from Jahorina Bistrica also passed through the Serbian zone of responsibility, supply which was never obstructed. On the contrary, the Serbian settlement of Grlica near Hrasnica was deprived of water-supply until the end of the war due to a blockage by Muslim forces situated in the Muslim part of Ilidza. Zeljko Bambarez explains that they set up a barrier with wooden planks, piled-up dirt, and blankets to thwart the attacks by enemy snipers. On one occasion, Zeljko Bambarez was targeted by a sniper belonging to the Muslim forces while digging a trench and the round hit the shovel and pierced it. Enemy snipers also killed an UNPROFOR soldier in Zeljko Bambarez's zone of responsibility and this UN soldier was transporting humanitarian aid for the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to ask you to look at some photos that you have already marked. Those paragraphs have to do with your own paragraphs, primarily paragraph 8 in your statement. Do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, I think we forgot to give an exhibit number to his 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D6904 receives number D2622, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at 1D8544. Can we zoom in on the lower part, the central part of the photo, where some markings have already been made. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bambarez, could you please tell us what is it that you have marked in this photo?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: In this photo I have marked two buildings. When I moved to Grbavica which was the zone of responsibility of my platoon in Grbavica. The first one is a red building. Can I perhaps point to it on the screen, this is the red building.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can Mr. Bambarez please be assisted with the photo. He should have shown the MEIS [as interpreted] in a different photo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it now. It is the notorious red building in Grbavica, the MIS. I marked the positions of the Serb forces as well as the position of the Muslim forces in that building. That building had five entrances, two were held by the Muslim forces and three were held by the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about letter M, what does it refer to?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the letter S?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: The Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us what is the building on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: The one with the blue roof?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Number 2.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Yes, number 2. That's -- that was a building that was destroyed during the war. Its appearance was not as it is now in this photo. The roof has been repaired. It was a building in front of our positions in the direction of the Unioninvest building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did that building prevent the view from the Muslim positions onto the streets across the river Miljacka?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: No, it did not. You can see that even in this shape and form that building is lower than the red building that was occupied by the Muslims, and during the war it was even lower than that. So there was an unobstructed view during the war even better than it is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is it that you marked by number 1?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Number 1 is a different building, the so-called skyscraper that was held by my platoon in the direction of the Unioninvest building.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness and the accused please be asked to make pauses between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did the building look like during the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could I remind you again that -- to put a pause between the questions and answers for the benefit of the interpreters and slow down. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did that building look like during the war, that building that you marked by number 1? Was its shape and form the same?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: The building marked by number 1 was not of that same shape. It was lower by some two floors. The building marked by number 1 during the war was approximately as high as the red building which I marked by letters S and M.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did it prevent a visual contact between the Muslim positions in the red building and the streets across the river Miljacka?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: No, no. Not the height that it was during the war because it was almost at the same level if not lower than the red building that was controlled by the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be assisted with the marking something with an electronic pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what is the street in the projection of these building on the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Do you mean the street that I'm now marking?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one. Can you put number 3 next to that line.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Yes, I've put number 3. I was not familiar with these little streets in Sarajevo before the war. I didn't know their old names. After the war, all of those streets have changed their names and none of them is called the same as they were before the war. I was familiar with Titova and Vojvoda Radomir Putnika Street, so the two main streets in the city, and the other two that I used to pass along often. I don't know their names. I read somewhere that today they're called Djure Danicica [phoen] and Zmjan Bosna [phoen], but I really can't say for a fact what their names indeed are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Towards the bottom and the right-hand corner can you put today's date and your signature.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit marked by witness receives number D2623, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D08546.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There seems to be some technical problem in saving the photo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is still on the screen. Can it be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are still experiencing some technical difficulties. Shall ... Could we do without the markings he made today? I think that's possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can, Excellency, as was originally planned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. If it is okay with you, then we'll admit 1D8544 as Exhibit D2623. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to call up 1D08546. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bambarez, after a break can you tell us what you have marked in this photo?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: In this photo I have marked a building that has been refurbished. After the war one floor was added to it and the sloping roof. During the war that building was not as high as you can see it now and it was not of such a lovely appearance, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you see in the background starting from the yellow cube-shaped building to the right.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: From the yellow cube-shaped building?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From that yellow building towards the Miljacka.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: From the Holiday Inn hotel you can see the Executive Council and in the background you can see the two buildings belonging to Unioninvest. Before the war they were called Momo and Zel [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where were the Muslim positions with respect to the building that you have marked? Do you see any part of the red building.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: No, in this photo you can't see any part of the red building.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, next exhibit. Exhibit D2624.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now I would like to call up 1D08555. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many floors do you see in this photo, the ground floor and six upper floors, right? We can all see that, can't we?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection. I just don't see it, so -- otherwise this is a perfectly inappropriate question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We're in a haste, I agree, but we -- I'm trying to move things along.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bambarez, can you tell us what this photo depicts?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: This is the same building that we saw in the previous photo but this was taken during the war. That was the building as it was during the war. It has been refurbished since then, but it is of the same shape as the photo -- as the building that we saw before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the number of floors that the building had during the war and the number of floors that it has received after the war?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: As I've already told you, that building, as we can see it now, was a bit lower than the red building, the building that I marked with letters MNS. After the war when it was renovated, we can see that it has become taller than it was during the war because now its height is different than it was during the war. The building is now higher than it was during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please ask the witness whether he knows who took this picture and from what angle and how he believed that this is the identical building we saw in the previous exhibit, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bambarez, how do you know that this is one and the same building?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Well, as I was looking at the previous photo where the red building was marked and the position of this building taken from that angle, you can see it's one and the same building but in a different shape and form.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And during the war did you ever come to this place?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: I entered the building because the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska were in this building. But we could not enter it from the side from which the photo was taken. We could enter it from the side, from the block of buildings that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know who took this photo?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, is this enough to admit this photo into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D8555 receives number D2625, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to call up yet another photo which is 1D08554, 1D08554.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what this photo depicts and what you have marked on it.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: This photo was taken from the Muslim side. We can see the Vrbanja bridge, the building of Unioninvest, and we can see the skyscraper building where the Army of Republika Srpska had its positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was it who held the white building of Unioninvest?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: That white building did not look the same during the war. It was a newly built building. There was only a concrete construction and it was under the control of Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted, Excellencies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this photo was taken after the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit it as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D8554 receives number D2626, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will not show the Baba Stijene photo because all it depicts is the rock and not a view from the rock. We will find another opportunity to show that photo. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
