utterances.text: And I take it you are not tendering other picture of blue roof, 1D8545, which is referred to in para 9?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I thought it was not in dispute. Obviously I would like to enter it. Can we call up 1D08545. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you see in the photo and what you have marked on it.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: The photo depicts on the left-hand side the renovated building which didn't look the same during the war. In the background you can see the Unioninvest building. As I've already told you, during the war it was a new concrete construction, so the building looked different during the war. The building with the blue roof was damaged during the war and it did not have the same blue roof construction as you see now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The position from which the photo was taken, during the war did it command a view of the streets across the river Miljacka? Where were Muslims forces in respect of that building?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: In respect of that building, the Muslim forces were in the red building which I marked. That building was held by both Muslims -- Muslim and Serb forces. And I believe that this photo was taken from the red building, from the part that was held by Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And as for the photos that you see in this -- as for the buildings that you see in the photo, where were Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: I know that some of the Muslim forces were in the Unioninvest building, and as for the rest of the positions I don't know where Muslim positions were in the depth of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With regard to the fact that a new part was added to this building, during the war did this building obstruct the view of the streets across the river Miljacka from the positions of the Muslim forces in the red building?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Can you please repeat, did this building what during the war? Did it obstruct --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, during the war did it obstruct the view from the Muslim positions of the streets across the river Miljacka?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Exhibit D2627. And the remaining five associated exhibits will be admitted into evidence and be given numbers in due course by the Registrar. I take it you have concluded your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bambarez, as you have noted, your evidence in chief was in most part admitted in the form of writing, i.e., in written statement of yours, in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to these photos.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 1D85544 -- 1D8544.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this is the photo of the entire city that you showed us earlier, and it's based off a photo in this area in the map book. And again if we can focus in on those buildings that you commented upon. So this building that we see with the red facade, this was held by both the Muslims and the Bosnian Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in your statement you've gone to some effort to show the heights of the other buildings, but I want to focus questions now as to where a Bosnian Muslim sniper would have to be posted in order to have a line of sight from off of the building with the red facade.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 1D8545, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, this photo was taken from the building with the red facade, the Bosnian Muslim building; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: I assume so. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, would you agree with me that it appears whoever took this photo had to be standing on the roof?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: At least on the last floor. If not on the roof, then on the last floor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can barely hear the witness. Could he please be asked to speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this is a building in which within the same exact building there are Bosnian Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: This building with the blue roof, the one that I see now?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No, my apologies. The building from which this picture was taken, the building with the red facade also had Bosnian Serbs in it as well, did it not?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so in order for your suggestion to make sense that there would be a Bosnian Muslim sniper on that building taking some action, that Bosnian Muslim sniper would be exposed to the Bosnian Serbs who were in the same building, would he not?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you about this building we see to the left, so not the blue building in front of us but the one over to the left. And you said today at transcript page 41, you said that the building with the red facade, the building from which this photo is being taken, was about the same height as the building on the left side. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: I said that the red building during the war was roughly the same height or slightly higher than the building that we see on the left-hand side than it was during the war, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And so for a sniper to successfully have a line of sight through that building that was of the same height or slightly higher, he would have to stand on the roof, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Well, you see, I came to these two buildings at the beginning of 1994, and the situation I found there is the one that I saw -- or rather that we saw in these photographs. 1994 was a relatively quiet year. The cease-fire was being observed. While I was at the front line and while I held these positions of the Army of Republika Srpska, I -- I don't know. I don't know of any sniper activity from that area, not even from the Muslim part. As for the Serb part of the building, there were no snipers at all. At the time we did not have any snipers. So I cannot say with any certainty that the Muslim forces were firing from that red building, that there was any sniper fire coming from there while I held the position I held in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So notwithstanding your testimony about the heights of all these buildings, you don't have any other information that there was ever a Bosnian Muslim sniper in that building, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: I don't have any information of that sort. I don't know of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to speak to you about your paragraph 7 which regards Osmice. And in paragraph 7 you say: "From the settlement of Breka, it was impossible to see a tank with the unaided eye ... in Osmice."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder whether the witness has his statement with him. Would you like to have one in hard copy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you can refer to paragraph 7 as well. And this is when you talk about Breka and it being impossible to see a tank with the unaided eye, "mainly because the road passes through a pine forest near Osmice and I don't think it would be possible to see a tank on grey asphalt in a green forest with an unaided eye at a distance of over 2 kilometres." Sir, how many tanks did your brigade have?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: I really don't know that information, how many tanks the brigade had.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: How about your battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: The battalion did not have any tanks at all. This was an infantry battalion, we were an infantry company. We did not have such heavy weaponry in our unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Would it be surprising to learn that your brigade had at least two tanks in this exact area that we're speaking about, in Zlatiste which is close to Osmice?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: The brigade did not have tanks stationed at Osmice.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What about Zlatiste, which is very close to Osmice, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Likewise, there was not a stationed tank there in the area of Zlatiste.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have P05941, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is a May 1995 document signed by Savo Simic. The Court's seen this before. If we can look at number 1, part (B), it speaks about fire support for the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade and the first thing it says is: 120-millimetre mortar batteries from Palez, an 82-millimetre mortar battery, and a 76-, and then it says two T-55 tanks from the area of Zlatiste and Vraca. Sir, seeing this now does this help you remember whether there were any tanks during your time in the SRK in Zlatiste?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, could we have the time exactly? Can we see whether the witness was there in the first place, when in May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: She told us the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was only May that was mentioned, not the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What's the year?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I suspect it must be a translation problem, but I did mention May 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which day? Which part of May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I think the witness can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1995 I was in the logistics platoon of the infantry battalion that was not at Zlatiste, and I was not present at Zlatiste in 1995 at all. What I said I said in relation to the period when I was in Zlatiste.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So other than the period when you were in Zlatiste you cannot tell us about any tank; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: That is correct, as far as the period when I was in Zlatiste is concerned; I can only speak about that. But I really do not have any information about the period when I was not in Zlatiste and I cannot state my views with regard to what you've said.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 1D8543.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is one of your photographs and this you say in paragraph 7 shows the Osmice feature as well as a view of the city and Breka from that particular feature. And if we can look at that just for a moment. So this is taken from Osmice; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: This picture is so unclear, so foggy. I cannot discern anything. I don't even know where it was taken from. But it is so unclear, the picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, have you seen this picture before?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Well, no, I haven't. But I see it now -- actually, I received it along with my statement and you can see even less there because it's black and white. So I really cannot discern this part of town, I mean the one that I see in this panorama in terms of this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, then I would strike this as an associated exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bambarez, could you expand on your statement that you received this with your statement in black and white. You stated just now that you received it along with your statement and you could see even less because it was black and white.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness is directing -- he's showing a copy of this in black and white just for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, would you like to respond to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think it would be appropriate to read out to him what is in paragraph 7 of his statement with respect to this and ask him if that is correct or not. And if he stands by it, then it should be admitted; if he doesn't, it can be withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bambarez, you said you had your statement with you. If you could draw your attention to the last part of paragraph 7. So at the end of that paragraph you were explaining three photographs, including 1D8543, which is the picture you are seeing in front of you now, show the Osmice feature as well as the view of the city and Breka from the feature. And then you said you thought it would be impossible to see a thing at such a distance with an unaided eye. So this is a photo you explained in your statement, but it's a bit difficult for us to understand that you can't recognise this photo at all. And I didn't understand what you meant that this photo came along with your statement. Does it mean you never saw this picture before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw this photograph before but I did not comment on this photograph with regard to the view from Osmice. I commented upon two other photographs, where you can see the Osmice pensione in a devastated state and also the plateau below Osmice. And I have those photographs in black and white as well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take this picture out of -- out from the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's continue to talk about Osmice and the view of Osmice into the city. Now, you've lived your whole life in Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: I was born in Sarajevo. I finished high school in Sarajevo. I worked in Sarajevo. But I lived on the outskirts of Sarajevo in a village that is about 7 kilometres away from the centre of Sarajevo. So I did not live in Sarajevo then but I got my education in Sarajevo, I worked there. My family home where I lived is about 7 kilometres away from Sarajevo, from the centre of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Then I suspect that you have seen the city of Sarajevo from views all around it in your lifetime?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Well, in my lifetime the best view of Sarajevo is the road from the town leading to my house and the viewpoint at the memorial park of Vrace. And that is the road that I saw most often because Sarajevo was a big city, after all. Your life goes by without going into each and every part of town. So I haven't been to each and every part of town from which there is a view of the city itself. So this is a view from the memorial park of Vrace, and you can see a considerable part of Sarajevo from that viewpoint.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But nonetheless in a little bit I'm going to be showing you some views of Sarajevo to see if you can help me with them in a moment. But first, in regard to this paragraph 7 when you talk about it being impossible to see a tank, do I assume that you're aware that the Trial Chamber has heard evidence from a witness regarding what she could see from her terrace in Breka, that she could see a tank in Osmice. Do you know about that evidence?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: The gentleman from the Defence team made me aware of that statement of that witness, who says that she saw a tank - I don't know when - on the Osmice plateau.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Now, I still claim that she could not have seen one.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So let's look at her evidence and then I'll ask you about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It's P00814, please, and if we can go to paragraph 25. P00814. This is the amalgamated statement of Fatima Zaimovic and let me just read you portion of this. It's paragraph 25. In regard to Breka she says it's: "... it's on an elevation above the town, so from my window I could see a part of Mount Trebevic and a part of the town, and I could even see those two large UNIS skyscrapers that were very badly shelled. Every morning, I could see a Serb tank move into position in the area called Osmice and start shelling the town. And on one occasion they even filled barrels with explosives and rolled them down to explode among the houses. I could see that from my terrace early in the morning. This must have been towards the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, when the shooting was fiercest. The tank was there all the time. There were only civilian targets being hit. I could see the tank shelling hitting houses and apartments. There were no military targets anywhere in sight. The barrels with the explosives were being rolled down from Serb-held territory in the area of Osmice." Is this the information that the Defence shared with you more or less?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: The Defence did not fully supply this information to me. They said only that there was this statement made by a woman who said that she saw from the area of Breka a tank firing from Osmice, firing at civilian targets in Breka. To this day I claim the following: If you look at the line between Breka and Osmice, it's about 2 to 2 and a half kilometres as the crow flies. In my statement I said, and we see that in the photograph here of the Osmice plateau --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: For the record you were showing 1D8542. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: If the tank was on the Osmice plateau, it would have to be here. There is a road going by Osmice, Lukavica-Pale. In my statement I said, and I say to this day, that on this asphalt if we look at the colour of the asphalt and the colour of the -- of a tank and the green forest around Osmice, I think that it is impossible to see a tank from that distance.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's look at 1D8541 which is the other photo you have in your statement regarding Osmice. And this is also from paragraph 7. This is Osmice as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When were these photos taken?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know when these photographs were taken, but judging by the way Osmice looks I see that this photograph was taken either during the war or after the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 24311, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to show you some other photographs that you've not seen before and the first one is going to be a close-up. And bearing in mind what that photo of Osmice looked like, I'd like to see if you see anything else in here. Do you see this photograph in front of you? It's taken of the Osmice area. And do you see that stone building on the left-hand side that's sort of above an orange-looking house, do you recognise that to be Osmice?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: If you could zoom in a bit, it would be easier for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If I can ask for assistance on zooming in on the stone building, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's been no zoom. It's still the way it's been except that you've lifted the picture up a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: How's that for you? Can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: I see the building. I see the contours of Osmice, but I cannot see the facade sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Then can you confirm for us then that that is Osmice?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: This picture was taken from the Muslim part. It was taken from the lower side of Osmice. I know Osmice better from the street on the upper side of Osmice and that's where I mostly entered, the one that leads to Pale --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: -- so I cannot say with any certainty --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can just go to the right a bit of the stone building of Osmice, and we see the pine trees and then we see a bit of a clearing. Sir, can you confirm to me that there was a road that went between Osmice and Baba Stijene?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And does that appear to be the road to you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in paragraph 7 when you spoke about your doubts as to whether somebody could see a tank coming from Osmice, you specifically said you thought it was impossible "mainly because the road passes through a pine forest near Osmice and I don't think it would be possible to see a tank on grey asphalt in a green forest with the unaided eye..." Now, sir, I want to tell you that this photo was taken very recently, in September of 2012. Would you agree with me that at the time of the war, some 17-plus years ago, the vegetation that we see in this photo would have been much less. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Well, regardless of the evergreen forest -- the vegetation is there all year round. These are evergreens. The leaves don't fall off. The pine needles are always there --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No, I understand --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: -- so it's --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters could not hear part of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You cannot even see the road from here. Would you like me to show where the road leads? You see how the road cuts through the forest here towards Baba and Osmice and now you can discern Osmice better than a moment ago. You can see for yourself what it is that you can see in any situation. There's even a gorge here above the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So -- thank you. So you yourself can see the road, can you not? You've just pointed it out.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: No. I showed it. Since I know the area. I don't know whether you can notice. You cannot see the road, but you can see this sort of canyon by the forest. I can discern that but I don't know if you can. So you see how it cuts through here, here.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think if the usher would switch on the witness's pen, that might be helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we ask Mrs. West to tell us what kind of zoom this is. Was this photographed at a ratio of 1:1 from the river?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's not a proper intervention, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, Madam Registrar, if we could -- before we were higher and to the right when the witness was speaking about the road, if we could go back to that view and then over to the right a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right, sir, you've got a pen. Show us what you were just speaking about. You spoke of a road. Can you point that out on the screen? You can actually write on the screen.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: I was saying that I recognise this part, but you can't see the street or the road. However, you can see where the road should be stretching through the forest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, we forgot to set the pen again. Just wait. Could you wait till assisted by our usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So now draw on the screen where you think the road is.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And can you also circle the building at Osmice?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you sign, please, sign your name on this and also date it, which is the 12th of December.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document receives number P6041, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, when you received this information, did they tell you that she looked out every morning end of 1992 and into 1993 and saw this tank?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: When I received this information - and I repeat, I only received information that there was a lady who had stated that she had seen a tank shooting from Osmice. I did not have direct reports myself, but I maintain that what that lady said is a complete fabrication. There was never any tank there. And she refers to the end of 1992/early 1993, that's the period when I myself was there at the confrontation line, and it's absolutely not true that there was a tank moving about there every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So putting aside your opinion of her observations, would you agree with me in a general sense that once somebody saw something once on one morning and they went back the next morning, they would more readily be able to look back at the same exact spot. And as each morning went by, they would more easily be able to spot exactly what they were looking for because they knew exactly where to look. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: I never did anything of the kind like observing something every morning, looking at one point, and looking to see something specific there. So I can't say whether I agree or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. In paragraph 23 you spoke about forced labour. May we have 65 ter 24337. And in paragraph 23, specifically you were speaking about Serb civilians who remained in Muslim area and were forced to do labour. Were there any occasions where you yourself were aware of the SRK forcing Bosnian Muslims into forced labour?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness sit closer to the microphones, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, could you just clarify that question for me, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Were you ever aware of Bosnian Muslims being forced to do labour by the SRK?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: On two or three occasions I was aware that a mixed-labour platoon came to us and helped us build protection facilities for the Lukavica-Pale road. Among them, I recognised my own manager, Serb by ethnicity, who was not a military conscript --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you this --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: -- and --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My apologies for interrupting, but we're under a little bit of a time-limit. You just said "mixed-labour." What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: I meant that when I recognised among the men in that platoon by Serb manager, I suppose that there were also Muslims among the members of the platoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's look at the document in front of you, and this is a document that's signed by you. It's dated December 31st, 1993, and it regards a working platoon from Grbavica and prisoners from Kula who were performing engineering works. It says there were a total of 15 people. Fifteen of them were working along the line longer than 500 metres. Sir, do you remember this incident or do you remember this occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And it says 15 of them were working along the line longer than 500 metres, does that mean the front line?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: That means the separation line on our plain where we held our positions. They helped us fortify our trenches and the shelters around the Lukavica-Pale road.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And as we go through it it speaks in the next paragraph specifically where people were working. And then in the middle it says: "In the morning Boro left to ask for the guards and he did not get any and he can confirm it." But then it says: "I remained at the locality where those people were working ..." So you were with them the whole time, is that right, or most of the time anyways?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: I was with them most of the time. Six men were working to fortify my trench and I spent the greatest part of the day with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And if we skip down to the bottom or the towards the bottom it says: "I was there for a maximum ten minutes and when I was returning," meaning you'd been away for ten minutes, but when you were returning, "Lackanovic was shooting at four of them who had started running away. Two more prisoners were at that spot and I managed to take them out of the communication trench." Let's stop there. When you made this observation, did you hear this Lackanovic give those prisoners a warning to stop before he started shooting or did he just start shooting at them?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: On the 31st December, as you see here, at 1600 hours, it was already getting dark. And I can see that we had called the command. Two or three members were working further down, members of the mixed platoon, and they were wanted for some other work further down the line --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, and I know that you're explaining the circumstances, but I think we can see it in the document. Can you just answer this: Did you hear him give a warning to the prisoners at whom he fired?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: I did not hear anything because I was far away from him. I couldn't hear him from that distance.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if we just go to the last paragraph this is what you wrote: "I just want to mention that regardless of all dangers that were in the places that are supposed to be guarded (during the day there were dozens bombs falling down a metre or two far from me), I was with them all the time until that moment." So here you're confirming that within that area where you were and where these prisoners in this working platoon were located, you were on the front line and you had dozens of bombs falling around you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: I state here that I was there with them and I built fortifications alongside them 50 metres away from the separation line, perhaps less, and the Muslim forces were showering us with bombs which were landing very close to us. So what I'm trying to say is I was there with them under the same circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Very good. And these people did not volunteer to do that work, did they?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know about the circumstances under which they were recruited, whether they volunteered or not, and I didn't even ask for them to come. They were brought there. And in addition to all the things we had to do, on the front line, we also asked for a security detail to come with these people; however, the security detail did not come. So we were forced to stay with them while they were building fortifications and we were together in the trench; however, they took advantage of the time when it was getting dark to escape and they escaped. Good luck to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, just one more question. Have you ever been a member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: I was a member of the Serbian Democratic Party of the Novo Sarajevo municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And during your membership, was that membership in 1991, 1992, 1993, about those years?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: I was a member of the Serbian Democratic Party in 1991 and the beginning of 1992 until the war began. The work of the party was on hold for the duration of the war so there was no party activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And my last question for you is: That information is nowhere mentioned in your statement, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Nobody asked me.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we remove this document from the monitor, probably you will tender this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it as next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document receives number P6042, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The English translation of this document, Mr. Bambarez, says that you were lieutenant-colonel at the time. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was your rank at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In June 1992 I started out as a commander of a platoon and then I became second lieutenant and remained in that rank until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So "p.por" should read "second lieutenant" instead of "lieutenant-colonel"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Your Excellency. May I call up photograph 2627, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were asked, Mr. Bambarez, whether you had noticed Muslim snipers shooting from the red building. I should like to ask you, were they able to shoot both from sniper rifles and even automatic weapons reaching the other side across the Miljacka river?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: They were able to fire with all infantry weapons across the Miljacka river from that building, including sniper rifles. But I said that during the time I was there I never observed them doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were they able to shoot from the Unioninvest building, that is, the white building?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get now P6041, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, is this area visible from the river without any special sights or is this picture taken with some kind of zoom?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: If we have noted that the distance between the Osmice plateau and the river is 2 to 2 and a half kilometres, I do not think that you can see this without using a zoom because you can see here very nicely these two buildings and the Osmice houses. So I don't think that using the normal lens of a camera you can get a picture like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we upload unmarked picture, the previous version, which was 65 number of which was 24311. So instead of putting the question to the witness, I think Ms. West could clarify whether this picture was taken with zoom or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Indeed it was, Your Honour, and I thought I had done that in the beginning, but it was taken with a zoom lens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried, Your Excellency, but you have instructed me about re-direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bambarez, with the assistance of the usher, could you please mark where the Serb and where the Muslim lines were. Can we see the Muslim lines on this picture? And who lived in these houses that we see close up?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: The houses that you see below the road leading to Pale were all occupied by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who controlled this area?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please use red and blue to draw the line indicating where both sides' trenches were.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: As far as Serb forces are concerned in this area, I can mark only that they were in the Osmice boarding house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about Muslim positions?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: This area is an area of rather steep slopes and they were somewhere here around their own houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you as a soldier say that there is enough range for a Zolja or an Osa hand-held rocket-launcher from the Muslim positions to the Serb lines?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It's beyond the scope of cross-examination. How does it arise from her cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Question -- then my question is: Would, Mr. Bambarez, as a soldier put a tank on the forward front line within the range of anti-armour weapons ?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Seeing that I'm not a professional soldier and I only have experience from the previous war, I would not put a tank on the forward front line nor would we need one. In view of the lay of the land and our own positions, infantry weapons were quite enough for our regular duties and sufficient to protect us. And I would not put a tank there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But would one be able to see a cannonball propulsed through the barrel of a tank, or rather, a shell?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: I don't know. How could you possibly see a shell from the barrel of a tank? God knows what the velocity is. I doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I'll read to you from transcript page 1980 from line 4 in English - you will get interpretation - that's my question. [In English] "But you said that you saw a tank and you even saw a shell being fired from the tank? "A. Yes, and the shell could be seen as it flew towards the apartment buildings there. "Q. But, Madam, that shell is fired at the speed of 1.300 metres per second? "A. Yes, unfortunately. "Q. So how can you see that? "A. But you can, you can see exactly how it's pulled and how it goes out -- how it's fired and the shell is fired from the -- that barrel." [Interpretation] What can you say about this? The lady says from a distance of 2 and a half kilometres she not the only saw a tank but also the shell coming from the barrel of the tank?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: That's simply ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you put a date on this photograph and sign it. You've marked on it Serb and Muslim positions.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: What am I supposed to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could you help him --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is your pen still active?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you put a date, 12.12.12, and your signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document receives number D2 -- just a second. D2632, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Just one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you provided your statement to the Defence team, when was it the first time you did it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Sometime at the beginning of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you shown all these photos at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BAMBAREZ
utterances.text: Some photos were shown to me. Until you show them all to me now, I can't say that I saw them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bambarez, for coming to The Hague to testify.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bambarez. That concludes your evidence. On behalf of this Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll rise all together. We're going to have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 25 past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.36 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sehovac. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Sehovac, before you start giving evidence, I would like to draw your attention to a particular rule here at the Tribunal. Under this rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the Prosecution or the accused or from the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in such a case, the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand you fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sehovac. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Colonel Sehovac.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you to take -- make a little break after my question. I have to remind myself of the same thing. This will allow the interpreters to interpret our words properly. Perhaps you could pay attention to the screen. When the letters stop moving the interpretation is over and you can start. Did you provide my Defence team a statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D6901 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that statement on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you read the statement and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does the statement reflect your words accurately?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, it does fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today in the courtroom, the same ones that were put to you by the team, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, may I tender the statement into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And how about the associated exhibits, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think we managed to get all of these on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They were on the 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there are several documents that were not translated? Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I haven't been made aware of that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There's one, Your Honour, at least. I believe one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I checked several days ago, but I had five of them -- six of them. What's the number, Mr. Nicholls? Good afternoon to you. What's the number that you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. 1D0675 from page 23 of the revised statement. That one I couldn't find.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. How about 1D8438, shall we upload it? I have to correct my statement. There are two or three documents that were not translated and the others were not uploaded on e-court, but let us check. Do we have 1D8438?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That doesn't look like it's uploaded on my e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. And how about 1D8446A?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we also don't have that uploaded apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about 1D20311 referred to in para 70?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Apparently we don't have a translation for that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And further, in para 53 the statement refers to 1D8424 and para 54 refers to 8425, i.e., 1D8425. The Chamber does not see these two documents as constituting indispensable and inseparable part of the statement. So if the accused is minded to tender those two documents he should lead live. And in addition to those two documents, those statements -- those documents untranslated and not uploaded will not be admitted at the moment. All the other remaining associated exhibits will be admitted and given numbers in due course by the Registrar. But before that, shall we give the number for his 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D6901 receives number D2633, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies. I'm not complaining, but I would like you to understand that this is not through ill-will of mine but through the lack of personnel. Even the few people that I have, who are exhausted, cannot keep up with the pace of work that has been imposed on us. I'm now going to read Colonel Sehovac's statement summary in English. [In English] Milorad Sehovac graduated from the land forces military academy, with a specialisation in infantry and the command staff tactical training school in 1990. He took over the duty of brigade commander of the 2nd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade around 18th of August, 1992. From June the 9 to July the 3rd, 1995, he had spinal surgery at the military medical academy in Belgrade. From 3rd of July until September 1995, he was in -- on sick leave. In mid-September 1995, he was transferred - due to the limited health capacity - to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command, as duty operations officer in the headquarters, where he stayed until mid-July 1996 when the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was disbanded. On April the 15th, 2002, Colonel Milorad Sehovac retired due to the operation with the rank of colonel. In the period between April 1992 and December 1995, the 1st Corps of BH army was in the part of the city of Sarajevo under the control of the Muslim authorities. These forces had units on the forward defence line, as well as support forces in the depth of their territory in the city. Unit of -- the unit of Colonel Sehovac had information that the 1st Corps of BH army has positions in civilian zones and civilian features. Neither in Hrasnica nor in Dobrinja was there any exclusively civilian zone without enemy firing positions or units. Superior command informed the UN about this by lodging protests. There were two basic objectives set by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps regarding the city of Sarajevo: First, protection of the territory and protection of the population. One of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps objectives was to blockade of the forces of the 1st Corps of BH army in the city in order to prevent them from being engaged on other fronts in BH. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps carried out active defensive operation and activity. His brigade partly carried out offensive activity exclusively for tactical improvement of positions. When carrying out combat operations, neither him nor his brigade understood those actions as part of a systematic or widespread attack on civilians. He heard about offers of the general headquarters civilian authorities and Dr. Karadzic himself for Sarajevo to be completely demilitarised. The Butmir airport was handed over before his arrival to the brigade, it was handed over for the humanitarian reasons and to serve the needs of the United Nations forces. Superior commands or civilian authorities informed his brigade about the provisions of the international law of war and humanitarian law during consultations and meetings which he attended, it was stressed and ordered to act in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. Dr. Karadzic personally insisted and demanded this every time. Orders from superior command and civilian authorities also stated that if fire was opened against civilians, investigations had to be carried out and perpetrators punished. But there were no such case in his unit. He also knows about efforts to enable the flow of electricity, gas, and water to civilians in Sarajevo, but this was under the purview of civilian authorities. He has knowledge that Dr. Karadzic personally strove to create normal living conditions for the Muslims who were in Serbian territory and to ensure the same living conditions for those on the other side of the front line. The brigade of Colonel Sehovac took preventive measures to avoid opening fire on civilian features. Action was only taken against observed combat positions and only when fired at. They did not open fire on civilian targets and if they knew there was a danger of causing civilian casualties, fire was stopped. Never he nor members of his unit or higher or lower commands had any intention of causing civilian casualties or terrorising or exerting psychological terror on civilians under the control of the Muslim authorities. He never issued, nor received, from superior commands or civilian authorities, any oral or written orders to carry out attacks against civilians or means of the public transport. On the contrary, superior command ordered - and so did he - that civilians in the city under Muslim control should not be targeted. Conversely, civilians in his zone of responsibility were subjected to direct sniper, mortar, and artillery fire by the Muslim forces on the daily basis, killing children, civilians, and soldiers, and there were cases of enemy sabotage groups carrying out raids and mutilating civilians. There were also rumours that Muslim snipers opened fire against the civilians in the city under their own, Muslim, control. Muslim units of the 1st BH Army Corps were supposed to be controlled by UNPROFOR, but this control was poor and UNPROFOR showed inactivity in preventing provocations from these units. Most units in the brigade of Colonel Sehovac were reserve forces and there were very few professional servicemen. The level of training depended on the period of war. In tactical actions, where proficiency of the unit was required, there were a lot of striking weaknesses. The lack of professional command officers affected the quality of control, command, and inspections of the brigade. Problems with the exercising of effective control were partly present. There were no specially organised sniper units in his brigade. Ammunition levels were critical and orders from higher commands insisted on sparing use. His brigade rarely had contact with humanitarian convoys, but it let civilians, for example, Croats go through its zone of responsibility when the conflict between Muslims and Croats -- Croatian forces broke out. He had information about the abuse of humanitarian convoys for military purposes for units of the 1st Corps of BH army. Most humanitarian aid goods went to the units instead to the civilians or were sold at the black market. These convoys were also used to smuggle weapons for the use of the 1st Corps of BH army. Colonel Milorad Sehovac had information about the existence of production of modified aerial bombs for striking targets on the ground which were in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps arsenal, but his brigade did not have them. He also had information about the modification of missiles for striking targets on the ground by units of the 1st BH Army Corps. He knows that there were no fuel air bombs in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps or JNA arsenal. There were no paramilitary units in the zone of responsibility of his brigade, and higher commands and civilian authorities were vigorously opposed to it. He had a good co-operation with the Ilidza and Trnovo municipality. He never obtained any information that there was a Serbian municipal policy of persecution, killing, or discrimination based on religious or ethnic grounds in the zone of responsibility of his brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the meantime I have some more information for you about some of these associated exhibits. 1D8438 is admitted already as P1208. I'm told that 1D8446A has been released. For 1D20311, we do have a translation. It hasn't yet been uploaded but it's being sent to the parties by e-mail, and we still don't have a translation for 126275.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Even for those documents the translation of which was now released -- yes, for that document still the accused -- Mr. Karadzic needs to lead live if he so wishes. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic. Thank you for the information, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I would like to call up 1D20311 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sehovac, do you have a copy of your statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please pay attention to paragraph 70 in your statement. Could you please tell us --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Why is he reading his statement? If he's going to ask him about the document, why doesn't he just ask him about the document. There's no more leading way than to go through the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic, when I said that you need to lead live, then why don't you put questions directly and put the document later on?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise. This is a novelty. This is a new experience for me so I need some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, were you in a position to bring your unit to full combat-preparedness and what was the occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I was often in such situations to have my unit in the state of full combat-readiness, especially when the enemy was preparing its offensives. Due to the shortage of personnel which is reflected in the order that is on the screen, we were forced to mobilise certain units on work obligation and those people who were employed in the bodies of authority, that's how we formed platoons and reinforced our battalions. The only reason for that was the shortage of personnel. Why was that the case? Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the location of our --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt and no offence to you, Mr. Sehovac, but I would prefer that this be done without the statement so we can test his recollection of the document. He's reading from the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can easily close the statement. So why did we engage those units? The brigade was mobilised from a very small area, Gojkovic [as interpreted], Grlici, and Kupres was that area, as well as the local commune of Kijevo. The average density of the population there was 5.000 inhabitants, and our strength was up to 70 per cent throughout the war, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm waiting for the interpretation to be over. Tell me, did you mobilise Muslims and Croats or did you only mobilise Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Those were purely Serb settlements. As far as I know in the local commune of Vojkovici there was only one Muslim family before the war. There was some Muslim families residing in Kasindol, but that was outside of my area of responsibility. Therefore, we recruited only Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, how often were you in a position to raise the level of combat-readiness to a higher level?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Let me just add something to my previous answer. In my unit there was only one Muslim throughout the war. When the war was over he went to Hrasnica and I also had a few Croats in my unit. How often was that? It depended on the combat situation at hand. There was a need to do that because the brigade occupied a special place in a built-up area and its position was tactically very unfavourable. Above the brigade, above the zone of defence of the brigade, Muslim units held a line of some 6 kilometres in a built-up area. They towered over the brigade and the distance in altitude between the two was about 250 to 300 metres. The area was wooded, intersected. The gradient was over 45 degrees, and we organised our defence in the field. And they could see us really well, and that's how they could open fire on us and that was the only reason we did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have in this area ambitions or mount any operations to expand your zone to include Hrasnica and some Muslim settlements?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: All combat operations carried out by the brigade were exclusively defensive in nature except for individual actions which I'll be free to say can be qualified as active combat operations, which means that on certain axes we carried out raids and incursions and sabotage actions against the forward lines of the enemy and we never engaged more than 100 men in such active actions. For certain activities we would second units one to two platoons in strength. We never attacked a Muslim-populated area. Ahead of the defence area of the brigade, the only Muslim settlements were Butmir and Hrasnica, and we never had any ambition to attack them nor did we attack them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now call up 1D20311. 1D20311.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, what kind of information did you get in mid-August 1994 and what does this document mean?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Can I use this, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's your document now.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Because the Prosecution showed it to me before. Yes, this is my document. It's dated 14 August 1994. It's based on an order from the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps five days earlier pending an enemy offensive we were expecting named Step by Step. I as brigade commander undertook all activities for all available forces in the area of responsibility of the brigade to be placed in a state of full combat-readiness, to carry out its tasks. We see under number 2 that two platoons were to be formed from the personnel having work obligation with personnel from the Famos enterprise. Men were to be taken to reinforce the 2nd Infantry Battalion. The 1st Infantry Battalion was to be reinforced with --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I would like to hear the interpretation of all the 15 points, but I would like to hear from you whether this information you had was correct. Did this offensive really happen in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, but I can't see points 9 and 12 on this page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably your question about 9 and 12 were not translated. Let's --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The speakers are both speaking too fast and overlapping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I just heard from the interpreters you are speaking too fast and do not put a pause between the answer and your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. We will try to make a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And I ask the same of you, Colonel. First of all, tell me whether this information you had was correct and did the offensive happen in August of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, the information was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please explain to the Chamber the gist of paragraphs 9 and 12. What I'm interested in is what kind of preparation this was for what kind of action and for what reasons.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Paragraph 9, the task is issued to the chief of artillery, Major Momcilo Gorancic to be ready to fire on targets on the ground and in the air. Since we had no artillery units, the brigade had mostly 120-millimetre mortars, Gorancic got the task to use a mixed artillery battalion of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade to establish co-ordinated action and plan fire on the eastern slopes of the Igman mountain. And in the area of the Sarajevo field, Sarajevsko Polje, from where we expected an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you look at paragraph 12 now and show us how many snipers you had and what their tasks were.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Paragraph 12, I'm issuing the task to battalion commanders to prepare their snipers, machine-gunners, and Browning gunners to successfully destroy enemy snipers and fire on detected targets of the enemy in their defence areas. The brigade had 17 snipers made in Yugoslavia M76 calibre, 7.9-millimetres. And these snipers were used in combat operations exclusively in places where their combat qualities and purpose could be used to best advantage, that means in open space, generally speaking, when the enemy was removed from the forward end of the barrage fire, mainly on the slopes of the Igman in a place called Rozice [phoen] and on the northern-eastern slopes of Bjelasnica and Treskavica mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are these populated areas? What kind of terrain was it? Were there any settlements?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: This is rugged mountain terrain, altitude ranging from 700 to 2.780 metres. There was not a single populated place in that part of the brigade's defence area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification pending English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D20311 receives number D2634, MFI'd, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, did you receive any working visits by the corps command and the UNPROFOR command?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. The corps command made scheduled inspections of units and based on perceived shortcomings issued tasks with clear dead-lines for these shortcomings to be redressed in order to improve combat-readiness of the brigade. And concerning the UNPROFOR, we did receive their visits throughout the war. And the UNPROFOR was particularly present after the Lukavac 93 operation when the brigade held positions between the area covered by the UNPROFOR and the area covered by the Muslim brigade. So that would be the period between 14 August 1993 when all operations ceased on Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was your attitude, the attitude of your command and brigade, to cease-fires?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: We observed cease-fires and honoured them to the extent we were not losing personnel and live targets. We only opened fire when the enemy fired first and inflicted losses upon us. You can see that from the documents of the corps command - and I hope you have these. And I can say regarding both the superior command and the UNPROFOR, we had a decent and honest relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the corps command verify your observation of the cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. In certain periods - and that happened constantly although not every day - they would send commanding officers from the corps command to check the combat positions of the brigade with the basic objective to establish whether we were complying with the ordered measures at the time of cease-fires.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Mr. Karadzic is kindly asked to repeat the number. He again did not make a pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They couldn't hear you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D6275.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Just a moment. I need to look through. This is a report from commanding officer Major Milivoj Solar who was subordinated to the corps command. And on 9 May 1993 he inspected some of the units of the Sarajevo Brigade. And he notes, as I'm reading this is the fourth paragraph from the top, Mr. Solar checked on the 3rd Battalion and toured all the positions of the companies in that battalion. It is said that they received an order from the brigade command to cease fire and they passed this order down. So the order went from the brigade command all the way down the chain. But then it is said that the order is fully observed on our side, and all violations by the enemy are regularly reported to the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Other things are noted here that I don't think are relevant to your question. So we see clearly from this document that there is full observation of the cease-fire by the 3rd Battalion of the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us - perhaps it's not important but it may give us a full picture - what was the ethnicity of this major?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: This was an honourable officer of Croat ethnicity. He remained with us until the end of the war and he lives in Novi Sad today and we still meet quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this inspection visit an exception or not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: It was a planned, scheduled, organised visit by a superior officer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I tender this exhibit and I'm giving up on the other two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D6275 receives number D2635, MFI'd, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, we won't be tendering 1D8424 or 1D8425.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. How about 1D8446A?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a map, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. There's no opposition with respect to that? Yes. That map will be added to the admitted associated exhibits. Then you're done, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Colonel Sehovac, as you have noted now that most of your -- all of your -- your evidence in chief in most part has been admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony, and now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Mr. Nicholls. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, I want to briefly go through some of the chronology of your military career that's left out of your statement, the same period we talked about on Monday. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I don't want to -- because of the time I don't want to spend a lot of time talking about all the different tasks you were doing, but just what your positions were. Now, in your statement in paragraph 1 we have -- you don't need to look at it, we have in 1990 you completed a two-year course in tactical school -- tactical staff command. You were then appointed as an assistant commander for a border battalion. That went until approximately August -- mid-August 1991. From mid-August 1991 to 16 July you were in Brcko as chief of a sector that was not a combat unit but a territorial organ dealing with training, mobilisation, sort of administrative things of that nature. On or around 19 of May, 1992, you became a member of the VRS. From around 16 July to 5th of August you told me you were Chief of Staff of the 1st Posavina Brigade in Brcko. And then on 18th of August, 1992, you became commander of the Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade, the 2nd, which we see in paragraph 2 of your statement and then it continues through your retirement. Is that correct how I've got the chronology?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. I do have a few corrections, though. I became assistant, not deputy commander of the -- that border battalion because border service is idiosyncratic. It took me seven months to be trained for the job and then the war began. I was not chief of sector. I was chief of military department. It is a military territorial department linked to the Ministry of Defence through the military district of Tuzla, and it doesn't deal with training as you said. It keeps records of military conscripts, it recruits, sends men to the army, and assigns military conscripts who have done their military service to military units of the former JNA, Territorial Defence, war time police, and other defence organisations under the then-system of All People's Defence. And I did not finish my career during the war. I went to the General Staff and later to the Army of Yugoslavia. I got retired on the 15th of April --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the year.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I finished my service in the staff of the command of the Novi Sad Corps. And I have one more thing to note. We need to clear this up. After the departure of officers from the territory of former republics on the 19th of May, 1992, I in the Brcko garrison, in addition to my regular duties of chief of military department, I also discharged duties of the Chief of Staff of the 1st Posavina Brigade. As far as duties of Chief of Staff of the brigade are concerned, I began with that as of 16 July 1992, when military departments were abolished and their responsibilities were transferred to the sections of the Ministry of Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- okay --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: -- that was established in municipalities. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to correct the transcript. Line 25 and on page 91 and beginning of 92, he said he was not assistant but deputy commander and he was retired in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now -- are you finished?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I please have up 24274.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'm going back to your time in Brcko now. I'm going to show you a document and then another document and ask you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I need e-court page 124, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, this is in English. It's only about one sentence, two sentences, so I'll read it out to you. This is from paragraph 327. And what this document is is the judgement in the trial of Mr. Krajisnik in this Tribunal. This is from the section entitled "municipality crimes." And I want to read out to you this part from paragraph 327 which deals with Brcko when you were there.
